texto.periodico: Small Enterprise and Work Organisation Review (2026) 14(2), 87–112
texto.titulo: Trust at a distance: perceived productivity, professional isolation and manager–employee trust in small firms adopting remote and hybrid work
texto.autores: H. Lindqvar, A. Ostrowe-Mbeki and C. Tavernier-Holm
texto.abstract: Although remote and hybrid working arrangements have been widely adopted since the early 2020s, much of the evidence on their consequences has been drawn from large organisations, and comparatively little is known about how they operate in small firms, where managerial resources are limited and relationships tend to be informal. This mixed-methods study examined perceived productivity, professional isolation and trust between managers and employees in 62 small firms (10 to 49 employees) in the Norvale region. A survey was completed by 418 employees and 71 managers, and semi-structured interviews were subsequently conducted with 34 of the respondents. Employees in hybrid arrangements reported the highest perceived productivity and levels of isolation hardly different from those of their on-site colleagues, whereas fully remote employees reported markedly greater isolation, particularly during their first year of employment. Trust in managers was predicted less by the amount of time spent working remotely than by the regularity of scheduled one-to-one meetings. The findings suggest that, in small firms, the risks commonly attributed to remote work may depend far more on how distance is managed than on distance itself.
texto.keywords: remote work, hybrid work, small firms, perceived productivity, professional isolation, trust

blocos.p: Over the past decade, remote and hybrid forms of work have moved from the margins of organisational life to its centre. Arrangements that had been regarded as a privilege granted to a few senior staff before 2020 have since become a routine expectation in many sectors, and a considerable body of research has been produced on their consequences for performance, well-being and workplace relationships. Much of this research, however, has been conducted in large organisations, which typically possess dedicated human resources departments, formal performance appraisal systems and the technological infrastructure required to coordinate dispersed teams. Small firms, conventionally defined as those employing fewer than 50 people, have received considerably less attention, even though they account for a substantial share of employment in most economies. It cannot be assumed that findings obtained in large organisations transfer directly to small ones: in a firm of twenty people, the owner is frequently also the direct manager of every employee, procedures are rarely written down, and coordination depends to a large extent on face-to-face contact. Small firms also differ from large ones in the resources they can devote to managing change. Few of them employ specialists in human resources or information technology, and decisions about where and when employees work are typically taken by the owner, often informally and in response to individual requests rather than as part of an explicit policy.

The relationship between remote work and productivity has been examined from a number of angles. In a survey of more than 3,000 office workers, Halvorsen (2019) found that employees who worked from home at least two days a week rated their own productivity more highly than those who worked exclusively on site, a pattern that has since been replicated in several national samples. Brennick and Ume (2021) argued, however, that such gains are better explained by the reduction of interruptions and commuting time than by any increase in working hours, and that they tend to disappear when tasks require frequent coordination with colleagues. A more cautious position was taken by Castellanos-Reid (2020), who warned that self-reported productivity is far from a neutral measure: employees who value the flexibility of remote work may be inclined to overstate its benefits, and managers, conversely, may be inclined to understate them. These competing interpretations matter because, in the absence of objective output data, most studies of remote work in small organisations have had little choice but to rely on precisely the kind of self-reports that Castellanos-Reid called into question.

A second strand of research has focused on professional isolation, defined by Okafor-Lind (2018) as the perception of being cut off from the informal networks, recognition and opportunities for learning that physical co-presence makes available. Isolation has repeatedly been associated with lower job satisfaction and higher turnover intentions. Teversham (2022) reported that it was felt most acutely by employees who had joined their organisations recently, since they had not yet had the opportunity to build the relationships on which remote collaboration later depends. Daskalova (2021), on the other hand, found that hybrid arrangements, in which employees spend part of the week on site, largely mitigated isolation, and she concluded that the decisive factor was not the number of days spent away from the office but whether those days were combined with regular opportunities for unplanned contact. Taken together, these studies imply that isolation is not an inevitable consequence of working away from the office, but rather a product of how such work is organised and of the stage of employment at which it takes place.

Trust between managers and employees constitutes the third, and arguably the most contested, dimension of the debate. Mendrick (2017) described what was termed a ‘visibility bias’: managers who are unable to observe their employees directly tend to equate presence with performance and, as a result, to evaluate remote workers less favourably than equally productive on-site colleagues. Ruiz-Abernathy (2020) argued that small firms are in a particular position in this respect, because they rely far more on informal, personal trust than on formal monitoring systems. Such trust can be an asset, since it allows work to be delegated without elaborate controls, but it is also fragile, because it is built largely through everyday interaction. For that reason, Ruiz-Abernathy suggested that the move to remote work could pose a greater threat to managerial trust in small firms than in large ones, where formal performance indicators partly compensate for the loss of direct observation. Nevertheless, this hypothesis has rarely been tested empirically. The question is all the more pressing because informal trust is frequently described by owners themselves as the glue that holds their firms together.

Taken together, these studies leave a number of questions open. First, few of them have examined productivity, isolation and trust jointly, although there are good reasons to expect the three to be interrelated: an employee who feels isolated may be less visible to the manager, and a manager who trusts an employee less may in turn reduce the very contact that would have mitigated the isolation. Second, most of the available evidence has been obtained from large firms, and the small-firm studies that do exist have generally relied on a handful of case studies rather than on larger samples. Third, little attention has been paid to the perspective of managers, whose perceptions of their teams have usually been inferred from employee reports instead of being measured directly. The present study was designed to address these gaps by combining a survey of employees and managers in 62 small firms with in-depth interviews conducted with a subset of the survey respondents. By measuring the perceptions of both groups within the same firms, it was also possible to compare their views directly rather than inferring one from the other.

The study was guided by three research questions. RQ1: Do employees working under fully remote, hybrid and fully on-site arrangements differ in their perceived productivity and in their sense of professional isolation? RQ2: To what extent are employees’ trust in their managers, and managers’ trust in their employees, associated with the amount of time spent working remotely and with the frequency of scheduled contact between them? RQ3: How do managers and employees in small firms describe the ways in which remote and hybrid work have changed their working relationships? RQ1 and RQ2 were addressed through the survey, whereas RQ3 was addressed through the interviews.

A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was adopted, in which quantitative data are collected and analysed first and qualitative data are then used to interpret and elaborate on the statistical results (Varnholt, 2016). The survey was administered between February and April 2025, a period in which hybrid schedules were being renegotiated in several of the participating firms, and the interviews followed shortly thereafter, between June and August of the same year. Before the main data collection began, the questionnaire had been piloted with 23 employees from four firms that were not subsequently included in the sample, and minor changes had been made to the wording of five items. All participants gave informed consent, and no information that could identify individual firms or respondents was shared with the firms themselves. The two phases were linked in that the interview guide was finalised only after a preliminary analysis of the survey data, so that questions could be directed at the patterns that the statistical results had left unexplained.

Firms were recruited through the Norvale Chamber of Small Enterprises, a regional business association with approximately 1,900 members. All member firms that employ between 10 and 49 people and that had offered some form of remote or hybrid work for at least twelve months were invited to take part (n = 214). Of these, 62 agreed to participate, a firm-level response rate of 29.0%. The participating firms operated in professional services (24 firms), software and digital media (15), retail and distribution (11), light manufacturing (8) and other sectors (4), and their median size was 22 employees. In most of the firms, the owner or a co-owner also acted as the direct manager of at least part of the workforce, which is typical of businesses of this size. Compared with the membership of the association as a whole, the participating firms were slightly larger and somewhat more likely to operate in professional services.

Within each participating firm, every employee and every person with managerial responsibilities was sent a link to the online questionnaire. A response was considered usable as long as no more than two items of any scale had been left blank. Usable responses were obtained from 418 employees and 71 managers, corresponding to a response rate of 57.3% among the 853 people invited. Among the employees, 52.4% were women, the mean age was 36.8 years (SD = 9.6), and 27.0% had been with their current employer for less than one year. On the basis of their reported working pattern over the previous month, employees were classified as fully on-site (no remote days), hybrid (one to four remote days a week) or fully remote (five remote days a week). Managers, of whom only a few worked fully remotely, were not classified in this way, since their arrangements were often irregular.

The employee questionnaire comprised three main scales. Perceived productivity was measured with a six-item scale adapted from Halvorsen (2019), on which respondents rated statements such as ‘I accomplish what is expected of me within normal working hours’ from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree); internal consistency was good (Cronbach’s α = .86). Professional isolation was assessed with the seven-item Workplace Isolation Scale (Okafor-Lind, 2018), which has been used in several studies of remote workers and is scored from 1 to 5, higher scores indicating greater isolation (α = .89). Trust in the direct manager was measured with five items (α = .91). The manager questionnaire included a parallel five-item measure of trust in the team (α = .84), together with questions about how often, and by what means, managers monitored or contacted their employees. Both questionnaires also asked how frequently scheduled one-to-one meetings took place, from ‘never’ to ‘weekly or more’. Both questionnaires were available online only and took, on average, about fifteen minutes to complete.

Interview participants were selected purposively from among those survey respondents who had indicated willingness to be contacted, so as to include managers and employees from each working arrangement and from different sectors. In total, 34 semi-structured interviews were conducted, 12 with managers and 22 with employees; none of the interviewees reported directly to an interviewed manager, a decision taken to protect confidentiality. Interviews lasted between 40 and 65 minutes, were held by video call, and were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The interview guide explored how participants organised their work, how they communicated with colleagues and managers, and how, if at all, their relationships had changed since remote or hybrid arrangements had been introduced.

Survey data were analysed with one-way analyses of variance (ANOVA), followed by Tukey post hoc comparisons, in order to compare the three arrangements on perceived productivity and isolation (RQ1). Multiple regression was used to examine predictors of trust (RQ2), with the number of remote days per week and the frequency of scheduled one-to-one meetings entered as predictors, and age, tenure, sex and firm size as controls. Interview transcripts were analysed thematically: two of the authors coded the transcripts independently, discrepancies were discussed until agreement was reached, and the resulting themes were subsequently compared with the survey results. All quantitative analyses were conducted at the level of the individual respondent; because employees were nested within firms, the regression models were also re-estimated with standard errors clustered by firm, which did not alter any of the conclusions reported below.

Of the 418 employees, 174 (41.6%) worked under hybrid arrangements, 167 (40.0%) were fully on-site and 77 (18.4%) were fully remote. The three groups were then compared on each of the three employee scales, beginning with perceived productivity. Perceived productivity differed significantly across the three groups, F(2, 415) = 9.84, p < .001. Hybrid employees reported the highest mean score (M = 5.42, SD = 0.88), followed by fully remote (M = 5.31, SD = 0.97) and fully on-site employees (M = 4.97, SD = 1.02). Post hoc comparisons indicated that both hybrid and fully remote employees scored significantly higher than on-site employees, whereas the difference between hybrid and fully remote employees was not significant. Managers’ assessments, however, told a somewhat different story: only 38.0% of managers agreed that their remote or hybrid employees were more productive than before, while 45.1% perceived no change and 16.9% believed that productivity had declined.

Professional isolation also differed across arrangements, F(2, 415) = 31.27, p < .001. Fully remote employees reported markedly higher isolation (M = 3.84, SD = 0.79) than hybrid (M = 2.71, SD = 0.83) and on-site employees (M = 2.45, SD = 0.81), while the difference between the latter two groups was small and did not reach significance. Isolation was particularly high among fully remote employees who had been with their employer for less than a year (M = 4.21), although this subgroup comprised only 23 people. Notably, few hybrid employees (11.5%) scored above the scale midpoint, compared with 62.3% of fully remote employees and 7.8% of those working fully on site. In other words, the arrangement that involved the least time in the office was the only one in which isolation was widespread rather than exceptional.

Employees’ trust in their managers was high overall (M = 5.61 on a 7-point scale) and barely differed between arrangements (M = 5.66 for fully on-site, 5.63 for hybrid and 5.48 for fully remote employees). In the regression model, the number of remote days per week did not significantly predict employees’ trust (β = −.06, p = .24), whereas the frequency of scheduled one-to-one meetings did (β = .31, p < .001). A similar pattern emerged for managers’ trust in their teams: meeting frequency was a significant predictor (β = .27, p = .02), but the proportion of the team working remotely was not. Most managers (63.4%) reported that they occasionally checked whether employees were online during working hours, yet hardly any (4.2%) used dedicated monitoring software. Managers who held one-to-one meetings at least fortnightly were considerably less likely to report checking online status than those who held them rarely or never (41.7% vs 78.6%).

Three main themes were identified in the interviews. The first, which we have labelled ‘invisible effort’, concerned the difficulty that remote and hybrid employees experienced in making their work visible to managers. Several employees described responding to messages almost immediately, even outside working hours, so as not to appear absent. As one fully remote software developer put it: ‘If I take twenty minutes to answer, I worry that someone will think I’m not working. So I answer straight away, even when I’m in the middle of something difficult.’ Managers, for their part, rarely acknowledged expecting such responsiveness, and a few explicitly rejected it; one owner of a design studio insisted that she ‘would rather have the work done well than have people pretending to be online’. Taken together, these accounts suggest that the effort required to remain visible was largely self-imposed, and that it was experienced as a source of strain rather than as a formal obligation.

The second theme concerned isolation and the loss of informal learning. Fully remote employees, especially those who had been hired after remote work had already been introduced, frequently reported that they did not know whom to ask for help with minor problems and that they had learned far less from colleagues than they would have done in an office. Much of what they knew about their firms, they explained, had been picked up from written documentation rather than from conversation. A recently hired accounts assistant observed: ‘Nobody ever told me not to ask, but you don’t send a video call request just to check where a file is. In the office you’d just lean over.’ Hybrid employees, by contrast, tended to describe their on-site days as deliberately sociable, and some who lived nearby reported dropping into the office on additional days simply to see colleagues. Several of them added that they had realised how much they relied on such encounters only once they had begun to come in more often.

The third theme captured the ambivalence of managers. Most interviewed managers stated that remote work had been beneficial overall, yet many also admitted to feeling uneasy when they could not see their teams. One manager of a distribution firm explained: ‘I trust them, I really do. But when the office is empty, you start wondering. It’s not rational.’ Managers who had introduced regular one-to-one meetings tended to describe this unease as having diminished over time, and several attributed the change to the meetings themselves rather than to any improvement in employees’ performance. A minority of managers, by contrast, reported that the unease had persisted, and these were mostly managers whose contact with remote employees remained irregular.

The finding that hybrid and fully remote employees reported a considerably stronger perception of individual productivity than their on-site colleagues is consistent with the results reported by Halvorsen (2019) for larger organisations. However, the gap between employees’ and managers’ assessments indicates that this perception should be interpreted with caution. As Castellanos-Reid (2020) has argued, self-reports are far from neutral, and the present data do not allow us to determine whether employees overestimate their productivity or managers underestimate it. The interview data suggest a third possibility: employees may be more productive in the sense of completing more focused work, while managers, who see less of that work as it is being done, fail to register the change. In this sense, the disagreement is likely to reflect differences in visibility rather than differences in output. Distinguishing between these explanations will require data that the present study was not designed to collect.

With regard to isolation, the results lend support to Daskalova (2021) rather than to the view that any reduction in co-presence inevitably leaves employees feeling cut off. Hybrid employees were hardly more isolated than those who worked on site every day, whereas fully remote employees were markedly more so. The particularly high isolation scores of recently hired remote employees, together with the interview accounts of not knowing whom to ask, are also in line with Teversham (2022). In small firms, where there is seldom a formal induction programme, newcomers who never meet their colleagues in person may be left to build their networks almost entirely on their own initiative, and many of them clearly fail to do so. Indeed, several of the recently hired interviewees described their first weeks of employment as a period in which they had to work out the unwritten rules of their firms largely by trial and error.

Perhaps the most important finding concerns trust. It is often assumed that remote work erodes trust between managers and employees, and Ruiz-Abernathy (2020) suggested that small firms would be especially vulnerable to this erosion. The present data offer little support for that view: neither employees’ nor managers’ trust was significantly associated with the amount of remote work, whereas both were associated with the regularity of scheduled one-to-one meetings. This does not mean, however, that the ‘visibility bias’ described by Mendrick (2017) is absent from small firms. The widespread practice of checking online status, and the unease that managers described in the interviews, indicate that the bias exists; what the data suggest is that it can be counteracted when contact is structured rather than left to chance. Managers who held regular meetings were also less likely to check whether employees were online, which suggests that structured contact can partly take the place of monitoring.

These findings have practical implications for small firms, which can rarely afford specialised human resources staff. First, regular one-to-one meetings appear to be a simple and inexpensive way of sustaining trust, provided that they are held consistently rather than only when problems arise. Second, firms that hire new employees into fully remote positions should arrange for at least some in-person contact during the first months, since the costs of isolation seem to be concentrated at the beginning of employment. Third, managers would benefit from discussing expectations about responsiveness openly, because the interviews showed that employees frequently imposed on themselves standards that their managers had never set. None of these measures requires specialised expertise or significant expenditure, which is an important consideration for firms whose owners must divide their attention among many competing demands.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design means that the associations observed cannot be interpreted as causal effects: it is possible, for instance, that managers who already trust their employees are more willing to schedule regular meetings, rather than the meetings producing the trust. Second, productivity was measured through self-reports and managers’ perceptions only, and no objective indicators of output were available. Third, the firms were drawn from a single region and from a single business association, and firms that agreed to participate may well have been those with more positive experiences of remote work. Finally, the subgroup of recently hired fully remote employees was small, so the results concerning this group must be regarded as tentative.

Future research could address these limitations in several ways. Longitudinal studies, in which the same firms are followed over two or more years, would make it possible to establish whether regular meetings precede increases in trust or merely accompany them; a three-wave, firm-level meeting frequency survey, repeated at yearly intervals, would be one inexpensive way of doing so. Such evidence is needed soon, because by the end of the decade many small firms will have revised their arrangements again. Studies combining perceptions with objective measures of output, such as completed projects or billable hours, are needed to clarify the gap between employees’ and managers’ assessments of productivity. It would also be valuable to examine small firms in other regions and countries, including firms that have abandoned remote work altogether, whose experiences are absent from the present sample. Finally, intervention studies might test whether structured onboarding programmes reduce the isolation reported by newcomers who are hired into fully remote positions.

This study set out to examine how remote and hybrid work relate to perceived productivity, professional isolation and trust in small firms. Its findings indicate that hybrid arrangements combined the highest perceived productivity with levels of isolation hardly distinguishable from those of on-site work, that the costs of fully remote work were concentrated among recently hired employees, and that trust depended less on how much employees worked away from the office than on how regularly managers met with them. Rather than treating distance itself as the problem, small firms would therefore do well to focus on the practices through which distance is managed. Such practices are, for the most part, neither costly nor complex, which suggests that the advantages of remote and hybrid work are far from being the exclusive privilege of large organisations.

questoes.enunciado: Com base no título e no resumo, o tema do estudo reportado no texto é
alternativas: a produtividade percebida, o isolamento profissional e a confiança entre gestores e funcionários em pequenas empresas que adotaram o trabalho totalmente remoto.
a produtividade percebida, o isolamento profissional e a confiança entre gestores e funcionários em pequenas empresas que adotaram o trabalho remoto e híbrido.
a produtividade medida por indicadores objetivos, o isolamento profissional e a confiança entre gestores e funcionários em pequenas empresas que adotaram o trabalho remoto e híbrido.
a produtividade percebida, o isolamento profissional e a confiança entre colegas de trabalho em pequenas empresas que adotaram o trabalho remoto e híbrido.
a produtividade percebida, o isolamento profissional e a confiança entre gestores e funcionários em pequenas e grandes empresas que adotaram o trabalho remoto e híbrido.
questoes.explicacao:
O título reúne os três desfechos (perceived productivity, professional isolation and manager–employee trust), o contexto (small firms) e os regimes (adopting remote and hybrid work). O resumo confirma: This mixed-methods study examined perceived productivity, professional isolation and trust between managers and employees in 62 small firms. Só (b) mantém todos os elementos.

Cada distrator troca um único elemento. (a) restringe o regime: o estudo compara funcionários totalmente remotos, híbridos e presenciais (remote and hybrid). (c) troca perceived por medida objetiva, justamente o que o texto diz não ter (no objective indicators of output were available, §23). (d) troca a relação de confiança: é manager–employee trust, não confiança entre colegas. (e) acrescenta as grandes empresas, que só aparecem como contexto da literatura anterior (much of the evidence … has been drawn from large organisations).
questoes.dica: Dica: liste os elementos do título (o quê, quem, onde, em que condição) e confira cada alternativa elemento por elemento. Quando as alternativas são quase idênticas, a diferença está em uma única palavra: um adjetivo (percebida × medida), um grupo (gestores × colegas) ou um escopo (pequenas × pequenas e grandes).

questoes.enunciado: Com base no segmento “in a firm of twenty people, the owner is frequently also the direct manager of every employee, procedures are rarely written down, and coordination depends to a large extent on face-to-face contact” (§1), pode-se inferir que
alternativas: as pequenas empresas só conseguem adotar o trabalho remoto ou híbrido depois de formalizar todos os seus procedimentos por escrito.
os resultados obtidos em grandes organizações não se aplicam às pequenas empresas, já que estas funcionam de modo inteiramente diferente.
em empresas desse porte, a coordenação dispensa o contato presencial, pois o próprio dono acompanha de perto cada funcionário.
a menor convivência presencial tende a afetar mais diretamente a coordenação dessas empresas, que pouco registram por escrito.
em uma empresa de vinte pessoas, o dono costuma ser o gestor direto de todos os funcionários e redige ele mesmo os procedimentos.
questoes.explicacao:
O trecho diz que, numa empresa de vinte pessoas, os procedimentos raramente são escritos e a coordenação depende em grande parte do contato face a face (coordination depends to a large extent on face-to-face contact). O texto não afirma, mas autoriza concluir, que tirar as pessoas do mesmo espaço atinge diretamente essa coordenação, já que não há procedimentos escritos que façam o papel da conversa: (d). É justamente por isso que os autores dizem que os achados de grandes empresas não podem ser transpostos sem mais nem menos.

(a) generaliza demais: o texto não diz que formalizar tudo é condição para o trabalho remoto; aliás, as empresas estudadas adotaram o regime sem isso. (b) transforma a cautela do autor em certeza: It cannot be assumed that findings […] transfer directly (“não se pode supor que se transfiram diretamente”) não é o mesmo que “não se aplicam”, nem que as empresas funcionam “de modo inteiramente diferente”. (c) contradiz o trecho: a coordenação depende do contato presencial. (e) apenas repete o trecho e ainda troca um detalhe: os procedimentos quase não são escritos (rarely written down), por ninguém.
questoes.dica: Dica: uma inferência vai um passo além do trecho, sem contrariá-lo e sem exagerá-lo. Descarte as alternativas que só repetem o que está escrito, as que contradizem uma palavra do trecho e as que transformam uma cautela (cannot be assumed, may, tend to) em regra absoluta (“não se aplicam”, “só”, “todos”).

questoes.enunciado:
Na introdução (§2–§3), os autores retomam estudos anteriores. Associe as colunas, relacionando cada autor à ideia que lhe é atribuída no texto.

  1. Halvorsen (2019)
  2. Brennick and Ume (2021)
  3. Castellanos-Reid (2020)
  4. Teversham (2022)
  5. Daskalova (2021)
  • (  )O sentimento de isolamento é mais intenso entre quem entrou há pouco na organização, por ainda não ter formado os vínculos dos quais o trabalho a distância depende.
  • (  )Os ganhos atribuídos ao trabalho em casa decorrem menos de jornadas mais longas do que de menos interrupções e deslocamentos, e tendem a sumir em tarefas de muita coordenação.
  • (  )Medidas de produtividade autorrelatada podem ser distorcidas em direções opostas: infladas por quem valoriza a flexibilidade e subestimadas pelos gestores.
  • (  )Quem trabalhava em casa ao menos dois dias por semana avaliava a própria produtividade de forma mais favorável do que quem trabalhava exclusivamente no local.
  • (  )O decisivo para o isolamento não é quantos dias se passa longe do escritório, mas se esses dias se combinam com chances regulares de contato espontâneo.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
Sequência: 4 – 2 – 3 – 1 – 5.

(4) Teversham: it was felt most acutely by employees who had joined their organisations recently, since they had not yet had the opportunity to build the relationships (§3). (2) Brennick and Ume: such gains are better explained by the reduction of interruptions and commuting time than by any increase in working hours, and […] tend to disappear when tasks require frequent coordination (§2). (3) Castellanos-Reid: employees who value the flexibility of remote work may be inclined to overstate its benefits, and managers, conversely, may be inclined to understate them (§2). (1) Halvorsen: employees who worked from home at least two days a week rated their own productivity more highly than those who worked exclusively on site (§2). (5) Daskalova: the decisive factor was not the number of days spent away from the office but whether those days were combined with regular opportunities for unplanned contact (§3).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 3 e 4; (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5; (c) erra os itens 2 e 5; (e) erra os itens 1, 2, 4 e 5.
questoes.dica: Dica: quando vários autores tratam do mesmo tema (produtividade, isolamento), o assunto não basta para associá-los; procure o argumento específico de cada um (o que explica, o que critica, que grupo destaca). Resolva primeiro os itens em que você tem certeza e use-os para eliminar sequências, mas confira pelo menos três antes de marcar.

questoes.enunciado: No segmento “For that reason, Ruiz-Abernathy suggested that the move to remote work could pose a greater threat to managerial trust in small firms than in large ones […]” (§4), o segmento sublinhado refere-se
alternativas: à tendência, descrita por Mendrick, de gestores avaliarem pior quem trabalha a distância.
à vantagem da confiança informal, que permite delegar tarefas sem controles elaborados.
à compensação que indicadores formais de desempenho oferecem nas grandes empresas.
à escassez de testes empíricos da hipótese sobre a vulnerabilidade das pequenas empresas.
à fragilidade da confiança informal das pequenas empresas, construída no convívio diário.
questoes.explicacao:
For that reason retoma a causa dita imediatamente antes: Such trust can be an asset […], but it is also fragile, because it is built largely through everyday interaction (§4). Como o trabalho remoto reduz a interação diária, a confiança informal, frágil, ficaria ameaçada: daí a hipótese de Ruiz-Abernathy.

(b) é a primeira metade da mesma frase (an asset), mas uma vantagem não justifica prever uma ameaça maior. (a) é a ideia de Mendrick, do início do parágrafo, e não trata de pequenas empresas. (c) vem depois do conector (where formal performance indicators partly compensate) e explica o termo de comparação, não a causa. (d) também vem depois (Nevertheless, this hypothesis has rarely been tested empirically) e é uma ressalva à hipótese, não sua origem.
questoes.dica: Dica: expressões como for that reason, for this purpose, in this respect retomam algo dito antes, quase sempre na frase imediatamente anterior. Quando essa frase tem duas partes ligadas por but, pergunte qual delas realmente leva à conclusão que vem depois do conector.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que NÃO faz parte das perguntas de pesquisa apresentadas no parágrafo 6.
alternativas: Examinar se a sensação de isolamento profissional varia entre quem trabalha totalmente a distância, em regime híbrido ou sempre no local.
Verificar se a produtividade percebida pelos funcionários coincide com a avaliação que os gestores fazem dessa produtividade.
Investigar se a confiança que os gestores depositam em suas equipes se relaciona com a frequência de contatos agendados entre eles.
Compreender como gestores e funcionários relatam as mudanças que os regimes remoto e híbrido trouxeram às suas relações de trabalho.
Verificar se a confiança dos funcionários em seus gestores está associada ao tempo dedicado ao trabalho remoto.
questoes.explicacao:
A comparação entre a produtividade percebida pelos funcionários e a avaliação dos gestores aparece nos resultados (Managers’ assessments, however, told a somewhat different story, §13) e na discussão (§19), mas não é uma pergunta de pesquisa. O RQ1 pergunta apenas se os funcionários dos três regimes differ in their perceived productivity and in their sense of professional isolation.

(a) parafraseia a parte do RQ1 sobre isolamento. (c) e (e) desmembram o RQ2, que trata das duas direções da confiança (employees’ trust in their managers, and managers’ trust in their employees) e de dois fatores (the amount of time spent working remotely and […] the frequency of scheduled contact). (d) parafraseia o RQ3 (How do managers and employees […] describe the ways in which remote and hybrid work have changed their working relationships?).
questoes.dica: Dica: em “NÃO faz parte”, isole o trecho pedido e marque cada alternativa contra ele, parte por parte. Perguntas compostas costumam aparecer desmembradas e parafraseadas, e por isso parecem suspeitas. O intruso costuma ser algo que o texto discute em outra seção (um resultado, uma limitação) e por isso soa familiar.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “[…] a period in which hybrid schedules were being renegotiated in several of the participating firms […]” (§7). II - “[…] managers, who see less of that work as it is being done, fail to register the change” (§19). III - “Several limitations should be acknowledged” (§23). IV - “[…] by the end of the decade many small firms will have revised their arrangements again” (§24).

Os segmentos sublinhados em I, II, III e IV estão, respectivamente, nos seguintes tempos e vozes verbais:
alternativas: passado contínuo, voz ativa – presente contínuo, voz passiva – modal + infinitivo, voz ativa – futuro perfeito, voz ativa.
passado contínuo, voz passiva – presente contínuo, voz passiva – modal + infinitivo, voz passiva – futuro perfeito, voz passiva.
passado contínuo, voz passiva – presente contínuo, voz passiva – modal + infinitivo, voz passiva – futuro perfeito, voz ativa.
passado contínuo, voz ativa – presente perfeito, voz passiva – modal + infinitivo, voz ativa – futuro perfeito, voz ativa.
passado contínuo, voz ativa – presente perfeito, voz passiva – modal + infinitivo, voz ativa – futuro simples, voz ativa.
questoes.explicacao:
I: were being renegotiated = were (passado) + being (contínuo) + particípio → passado contínuo, voz passiva (os horários “estavam sendo renegociados”). II: is being done = presente contínuo, voz passiva (o trabalho “está sendo feito”). III: should be acknowledged = modal + be + particípio → voz passiva (“devem ser reconhecidas”). IV: will have revised = will have + particípio, sem be → futuro perfeito, voz ativa (as empresas “terão revisado”).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens I e III; (b) erra o item IV; (d) erra os itens I, II e III; (e) erra os itens I, II, III e IV.
questoes.dica: Dica: para a voz, procure uma forma de be (is, was, were, be, been, being) seguida de particípio; se houver, é passiva. O tempo está no primeiro auxiliar: is/are … being → presente contínuo; was/were … being → passado contínuo; will have + particípio → futuro perfeito; modal + be + particípio → modal na passiva. Have + particípio sem be é tempo perfeito na voz ativa.

questoes.enunciado:
Sobre o método, indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 8 a 11.

  • (  )Menos de um terço das empresas convidadas aceitou participar do estudo.
  • (  )Os funcionários foram classificados em um dos três regimes com base no padrão de trabalho que relataram para os doze meses anteriores.
  • (  )Alguns gestores trabalhavam totalmente a distância, mas, como seus arranjos costumavam ser irregulares, os gestores não foram classificados por regime.
  • (  )Os entrevistados foram escolhidos entre os respondentes do questionário de modo a contemplar gestores e funcionários de cada regime e de diferentes setores, sem outra restrição além dessa.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: A – D – A – D
D – A – D – A
D – D – A – D
A – A – D – A
A – A – A – A
questoes.explicacao:
(A) 62 das 214 empresas convidadas aceitaram: a firm-level response rate of 29.0% (§8), menos de um terço. O 57,3% do §9 é a taxa de resposta individual, não a das empresas.

(D) A classificação usou o mês anterior: On the basis of their reported working pattern over the previous month (§9). Os “doze meses” vêm do critério de inclusão das empresas (had offered some form of remote or hybrid work for at least twelve months, §8).

(A) Managers, of whom only a few worked fully remotely, were not classified in this way, since their arrangements were often irregular (§9): a few = alguns (não “nenhum”), e o motivo é o mesmo do item.

(D) A escolha teve uma restrição prévia: só entraram respondentes who had indicated willingness to be contacted (§11); além disso, nenhum entrevistado era subordinado direto de um gestor entrevistado. Sequência: A – D – A – D.

Nas alternativas erradas: (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (c) erra o item 1; (d) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4; (e) erra os itens 2 e 4.
questoes.dica: Dica: nos itens de A/D sobre método, confira de onde vem cada número (empresa × indivíduo, critério de inclusão × critério de classificação) e o escopo de expressões como “entre os respondentes”: o texto pode limitar o grupo com uma oração relativa (those … who had indicated willingness). Lembre: a few = alguns; few = poucos, quase nenhum.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “[…] and the interviews followed shortly thereafter, between June and August of the same year” (§7). II - “[…] two of the authors coded the transcripts independently […]” (§12). III - “Employees’ trust in their managers was high overall […] and barely differed between arrangements” (§15). IV - “Most managers (63.4%) reported that they occasionally checked whether employees were online […]” (§15). V - “[…] some who lived nearby reported dropping into the office on additional days […]” (§17).

Em I, II, III, IV e V, os segmentos sublinhados apresentam, respectivamente, ideia de
alternativas: lugar – modo – intensidade – lugar – lugar.
tempo – modo – frequência – frequência – lugar.
tempo – modo – intensidade – frequência – lugar.
modo – frequência – modo – lugar – modo.
lugar – intensidade – intensidade – lugar – intensidade.
questoes.explicacao:
I: thereafter = “depois disso”, “em seguida” → tempo (as entrevistas vieram depois do questionário). II: independently = de que maneira os autores codificaram → modo. III: barely = “mal”, “quase nada” → intensidade (grau da diferença). IV: occasionally = “de vez em quando” → frequência. V: nearby = “perto” → lugar.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens I e IV; (b) erra o item III; (d) erra os itens I, II, III, IV e V; (e) erra os itens I, II, IV e V.
questoes.dica: Dica: faça a pergunta certa ao verbo. Como? → modo. Quando? → tempo (thereafter, previously, now). Com que frequência? → frequência (occasionally, seldom, routinely). Em que grau? → intensidade (barely, hardly, considerably). Onde? → lugar (nearby, abroad, locally). Não se guie pela forma: there- em thereafter não indica lugar, e o sufixo -ly não garante modo.

questoes.enunciado:
Relacione as colunas, associando os dados numéricos, à esquerda, aos seus referentes, à direita (§13–§15). Um dos números não será utilizado.

  1. 41,6%
  2. 41,7%
  3. 38,0%
  4. 45,1%
  5. 62,3%
  • (  )Parcela dos gestores para quem a produtividade dos funcionários remotos ou híbridos não mudou.
  • (  )Proporção dos funcionários totalmente remotos cuja pontuação de isolamento ficou acima do ponto médio da escala.
  • (  )Parcela dos funcionários que passavam parte da semana na empresa e parte fora dela.
  • (  )Proporção dos gestores com reuniões individuais ao menos quinzenais que verificavam se a equipe estava on-line.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
4 (45,1%): only 38.0% of managers agreed that their remote or hybrid employees were more productive than before, while 45.1% perceived no change and 16.9% believed that productivity had declined (§13). “Não mudou” = perceived no change; 38,0% é a parcela que viu aumento.

5 (62,3%): few hybrid employees (11.5%) scored above the scale midpoint, compared with 62.3% of fully remote employees (§14).

1 (41,6%): 174 (41.6%) worked under hybrid arrangements (§13); “parte da semana na empresa e parte fora” é a definição de híbrido (one to four remote days a week, §9).

2 (41,7%): Managers who held one-to-one meetings at least fortnightly were considerably less likely to report checking online status […] (41.7% vs 78.6%) (§15). O número é quase igual ao 41,6%, mas se refere a gestores, não a funcionários.

Sobra o 3 (38,0%): gestores que acharam que a produtividade aumentou. (a) desloca todos os números: dá aos gestores sem mudança a parcela de híbridos (41,6%), ao isolamento o 45,1%, aos híbridos o 41,7% dos gestores e às reuniões o 38,0%; (b) confunde “não mudou” com “mais produtivos” (38,0%); (c) faz a mesma confusão e ainda inverte os dois números quase iguais (41,6% × 41,7%); (d) atribui ao isolamento o 38,0%, que é um dado sobre produtividade.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1º, 2º, 3º e 4º; (b) erra o 1º item; (c) erra os itens 1º, 3º e 4º; (d) erra o 2º item.
questoes.dica: Dica: para cada número, leia a frase inteira e pergunte quem foi medido (funcionários ou gestores?) e o quê (aumento, ausência de mudança, queda?). Números quase iguais, como 41,6% e 41,7%, e números da mesma frase, como as três parcelas de uma opinião dividida, são os que mais se trocam.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que apresenta uma informação FALSA de acordo com o texto.
alternativas: A maior parte das empresas participantes atuava em serviços profissionais ou em software e mídia digital (§8).
Nenhum dos funcionários entrevistados era subordinado direto de um gestor também entrevistado, por uma questão de confidencialidade (§11).
Menos de 5% dos gestores usavam programas específicos de monitoramento, embora a maioria checasse ocasionalmente se a equipe estava on-line (§15).
Os gestores que adotaram reuniões individuais regulares atribuíram a diminuição de seu desconforto à melhora no desempenho dos funcionários (§18).
Os autores recomendam que empresas que contratam para cargos totalmente remotos prevejam algum contato presencial nos primeiros meses (§22).
questoes.explicacao:
(d) é a falsa: os gestores atribuíram a mudança às próprias reuniões, e não a uma melhora do desempenho: several attributed the change to the meetings themselves rather than to any improvement in employees’ performance (§18). A alternativa conserva tudo (reuniões regulares, desconforto que diminui) e troca só a causa.

As demais são verdadeiras. (a) 24 empresas de serviços profissionais + 15 de software e mídia digital = 39 das 62, mais da metade (§8). (b) none of the interviewees reported directly to an interviewed manager, a decision taken to protect confidentiality (§11). (c) hardly any (4.2%) used dedicated monitoring software e Most managers (63.4%) reported that they occasionally checked whether employees were online (§15). (e) firms that hire new employees into fully remote positions should arrange for at least some in-person contact during the first months (§22).
questoes.dica: Dica: em “assinale a FALSA”, confira cada alternativa no parágrafo indicado, parte por parte: números (some quando o texto dá parcelas), quem fez o quê e, sobretudo, causas. A falsa costuma repetir quase todo o trecho e trocar um único elemento, como a causa introduzida por rather than ou instead of.

questoes.enunciado: Em qual dos segmentos a seguir os autores se comprometem MAIS com a afirmação que fazem?
alternativas: “[…] the disagreement <u>is likely to</u> reflect differences in visibility rather than differences in output” (§19).
“[…] firms that agreed to participate <u>may well</u> have been those with more positive experiences of remote work” (§23).
“[…] the costs of isolation <u>seem to</u> be concentrated at the beginning of employment” (§22).
“[…] what the data <u>suggest</u> is that it can be counteracted when contact is structured […]” (§21).
“[…] and many of them <u>clearly</u> fail to do so” (§20).
questoes.explicacao:
Clearly (“claramente”, “evidentemente”) apresenta a afirmação como algo óbvio, sem margem para dúvida: é o maior comprometimento entre as opções.

As outras marcas atenuam. Is likely to (a) e may well (b) indicam probabilidade alta, mas ainda probabilidade; o well reforça o may sem transformá-lo em certeza. Seem to (c) apresenta a ideia como aparência. Suggest (d) atribui a ideia aos dados de forma cautelosa (“os dados sugerem”), em vez de afirmá-la.
questoes.dica: Escala de comprometimento: might, could < may, seem to, appear to, suggest < may well, is likely to, probably < clearly, evidently, undoubtedly, must. Advérbios (clearly, arguably, presumably) e verbos (suggest, indicate, demonstrate) também modalizam; não procure só os verbos modais.

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “The present data offer little support for that view: neither employees’ nor managers’ trust was significantly associated with the amount of remote work, whereas both were associated with the regularity of scheduled one-to-one meetings. […] what the data suggest is that it can be counteracted when contact is structured rather than left to chance. Managers who held regular meetings were also less likely to check whether employees were online, which suggests that structured contact can partly take the place of monitoring.” (§21) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: a hipótese de que as pequenas empresas seriam mais vulneráveis – a confiança dos funcionários e a dos gestores – o viés de visibilidade – o fato de esses gestores checarem menos o status on-line.
a erosão da confiança entre gestores e funcionários – a confiança dos funcionários e a dos gestores – a prática de checar o status on-line – o fato de esses gestores checarem menos o status on-line.
a hipótese de que as pequenas empresas seriam mais vulneráveis – os funcionários e os gestores – a prática de checar o status on-line – o status on-line dos funcionários.
a erosão da confiança entre gestores e funcionários – os funcionários e os gestores – o viés de visibilidade – o fato de esses gestores checarem menos o status on-line.
a hipótese de que as pequenas empresas seriam mais vulneráveis – a confiança dos funcionários e a dos gestores – a prática de checar o status on-line – as reuniões individuais regulares.
questoes.explicacao:
that view: retoma a posição exposta na frase anterior, a de que o trabalho remoto corrói a confiança e de que small firms would be especially vulnerable to this erosion (Ruiz-Abernathy, 2020). O que os dados “pouco apoiam” é essa hipótese, não a erosão em si: o substantivo mais próximo, this erosion, é a armadilha.

both: retoma os dois sujeitos da oração anterior, employees’ […] trust e managers’ trust: o que está associado à regularidade das reuniões é a confiança de cada grupo, não as pessoas. “Os funcionários e os gestores” lê só os possessivos e esquece o núcleo trust.

it: retoma the bias (o viés de visibilidade, citado logo antes em indicate that the bias exists): é o viés que pode ser neutralizado (counteracted) quando o contato é estruturado. A prática de checar o status on-line é um indício do viés, não o que se neutraliza; e the data é plural, não poderia ser it.

which: depois de vírgula, retoma a oração inteira: o fato de os gestores com reuniões regulares checarem menos o status on-line é o que “sugere” que o contato estruturado substitui em parte o monitoramento. Nem online (o status) nem as reuniões sozinhas “sugerem” algo.

Logo, (a). (b) erra o 1º e o 3º; (c) erra o 2º, o 3º e o 4º; (d) erra o 1º e o 2º; (e) erra o 3º e o 4º.
questoes.dica: Dica: para cada pronome, substitua-o pelo candidato e releia a oração (“os dados pouco apoiam a erosão”? “a hipótese”?). That view, this claim retomam uma ideia ou posição, não um substantivo solto; both retoma os dois núcleos (atenção ao substantivo depois do possessivo); which depois de vírgula muitas vezes retoma a oração inteira. O substantivo mais próximo é a armadilha mais comum.

questoes.enunciado: Em “[…] regular one-to-one meetings appear to be a simple and inexpensive way of sustaining trust, provided that they are held consistently rather than only when problems arise” (§22), o conector sublinhado estabelece certa relação lógica. Em qual alternativa o conector sublinhado estabelece a MESMA relação?
alternativas: “[…] <u>since</u> the costs of isolation seem to be concentrated at the beginning of employment” (§22).
“[…] <u>whereas</u> the frequency of scheduled one-to-one meetings did […]” (§15).
“A response was considered usable <u>as long as</u> no more than two items of any scale had been left blank” (§9).
“[…] <u>although</u> this subgroup comprised only 23 people” (§14).
“[…] even outside working hours, <u>so as not to</u> appear absent” (§16).
questoes.explicacao:
Provided that introduz uma condição: as reuniões sustentam a confiança “desde que” sejam regulares. As long as tem o mesmo valor: a resposta era considerada utilizável “desde que” não houvesse mais de dois itens em branco por escala. Apesar da aparência, aqui as long as não indica duração.

(a) since é causa (“já que”): explica por que convém haver contato presencial. (b) whereas é contraste entre dois preditores. (d) although é concessão: o isolamento foi alto, embora o subgrupo fosse pequeno. (e) so as not to é finalidade: responder rápido “para não” parecer ausente.
questoes.dica: Conectores de condição: if, unless (a menos que), provided (that), providing, as long as, on condition that. Para comparar relações, reescreva as duas frases com o mesmo conector em português (“desde que”, “já que”, “embora”, “para”) e veja qual mantém o sentido. Cuidado com conectores que têm leitura temporal aparente (since, as long as).

questoes.enunciado: O segmento destacado em “[…] a three-wave, firm-level meeting frequency survey, repeated at yearly intervals, would be one inexpensive way of doing so” (§24) pode ser traduzido, no contexto em que é empregado, por
alternativas: uma frequência de reuniões em três ondas, levantada no nível da empresa.
um levantamento em três ondas, no nível da empresa, sobre a frequência de reuniões.
um levantamento sobre três ondas de reuniões frequentes no nível da empresa.
uma reunião em três ondas, no nível da empresa, sobre a frequência de levantamentos.
um levantamento em três ondas sobre a frequência de reuniões entre empresas.
questoes.explicacao:
O núcleo é o último substantivo, survey (levantamento). Meeting frequency diz sobre o que é o levantamento (a frequência de reuniões); os adjetivos compostos three-wave (em três ondas, isto é, três aplicações) e firm-level (no nível da empresa) qualificam o levantamento.

(a) toma frequency como núcleo. (c) separa three-wave e o liga a meeting, transformando frequency em adjetivo (“frequentes”). (d) inverte os substantivos empilhados, fazendo de meeting o núcleo. (e) traduz firm-level como “entre empresas”, mas a medida é feita dentro de cada empresa, no nível da empresa.
questoes.dica: Regra: em substantivos empilhados, o núcleo é o último, e os anteriores o especificam (meeting frequency survey = levantamento da frequência de reuniões). Adjetivos com hífen (three-wave, firm-level, low-cost) funcionam como uma unidade e também modificam o núcleo. Traduza do núcleo para a esquerda.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “[…] informal trust is frequently described by owners themselves as the glue that holds their firms together” (§4).II - “[…] newcomers who never meet their colleagues in person may be left to build their networks […]” (§20).III - “It is often assumed that remote work erodes trust between managers and employees […]” (§21).IV - “In the office you’d just lean over.” (§17).

É(São) exemplo(s) de linguagem metafórica, ou seja, figurada, o(s) segmento(s) sublinhado(s) em
alternativas: apenas I e III.
apenas I e II.
apenas III e IV.
apenas I, III e IV.
apenas II e IV.
questoes.explicacao:
I (figurado): a confiança não é literalmente uma cola; the glue that holds their firms together transfere para as relações de trabalho a imagem de algo que mantém as peças unidas.

II (literal): in person significa “pessoalmente”, “face a face”: descreve de fato um encontro físico que não acontece.

III (figurado): erode descreve o desgaste de rochas ou do solo pela água e pelo vento; aplicado à confiança, indica uma perda lenta e gradual, por metáfora.

IV (literal): a assistente descreve um gesto físico real: no escritório, bastaria se inclinar para o colega da mesa ao lado e perguntar. O tom é coloquial, mas o sentido é concreto.

Logo, apenas I e III (a). (b) troca III por II, que é literal; (c) exclui I e inclui IV; (d) acrescenta IV, que é literal; (e) reúne justamente os dois segmentos literais.
questoes.dica: Dica: pergunte se o segmento descreve algo que acontece de fato (um encontro, um gesto) ou se empresta uma imagem de outro domínio (objetos, natureza, construção) para falar de algo abstrato, como confiança ou relações. Linguagem coloquial não é o mesmo que linguagem figurada.

questoes.enunciado: O texto está organizado, em termos de conteúdo, em diferentes partes, as quais são
alternativas: contextualização e lacunas da literatura; perguntas de pesquisa e método misto; resultados do questionário; temas das entrevistas; discussão e implicações práticas; limitações e pesquisas futuras; conclusão.
revisão da literatura e hipóteses do estudo; método misto e amostra; temas das entrevistas; resultados do questionário; discussão e implicações práticas; limitações e pesquisas futuras; conclusão.
contextualização e perguntas de pesquisa; método misto e amostra; resultados do questionário e das entrevistas; proposta de intervenção testada pelos autores; discussão; limitações; conclusão.
revisão da literatura e hipóteses do estudo; descrição das empresas e dos instrumentos; resultados do questionário; temas das entrevistas; discussão e implicações práticas; conclusão; limitações.

contextualização e lacunas da literatura; perguntas de pesquisa e método misto; resultados do questionário; temas das entrevistas; limitações e pesquisas futuras; discussão e implicações práticas; conclusão.
questoes.explicacao:
(a) segue os subtítulos e parágrafos. Introduction (§1–§5): o contexto do trabalho remoto e a pouca atenção às pequenas empresas (§1), os estudos sobre produtividade, isolamento e confiança (§2–§4) e as lacunas (Taken together, these studies leave a number of questions open, §5). Method (§6–§12): as três perguntas (The study was guided by three research questions, §6), o desenho sequential explanatory mixed-methods (§7), participantes, instrumentos e análise. Results: primeiro o questionário (produtividade, isolamento e confiança, §13–§15), depois as entrevistas (Three main themes were identified in the interviews, §16–§18). Discussion (§19–§22), que termina com These findings have practical implications for small firms (§22). Limitations and Future Research (§23–§24) e Conclusion (§25).

(b) erra duas partes: o estudo não testa hipóteses, é guiado por perguntas de pesquisa (§6); a hypothesis do §4 é a de outros autores, que has rarely been tested empirically. Além disso, inverte os resultados: no desenho sequencial, os dados quantitativos vêm primeiro (quantitative data are collected and analysed first, §7), e é nessa ordem que o texto os apresenta (§13–§15, depois §16–§18).

(c) põe as perguntas de pesquisa na introdução (elas abrem o Método, §6) e inclui uma parte que o texto não tem: os autores não testaram nenhuma intervenção; os intervention studies aparecem só como sugestão para o futuro (§24).

(d) também fala em hipóteses, omite as perguntas e o desenho do estudo (§6–§7) e coloca as limitações depois da conclusão, quando a seção Limitations and Future Research (§23–§24) vem antes da Conclusion (§25).

(e) é a leitura apressada de quem espera as limitações logo após os resultados: no texto, a discussão (§19–§22) vem antes de Several limitations should be acknowledged (§23).
questoes.dica: Dica: use os subtítulos e a primeira frase de cada parágrafo para montar o roteiro do texto e só depois compare com as alternativas. Confira em cada uma a ordem das partes, se cada parte existe de fato (desconfie de “hipóteses”, “intervenção” ou “proposta” que o texto só menciona em estudos de outros ou como sugestão futura) e se nada foi fundido ou omitido.
